To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transcriptomic signature of ant queens is distinct from that of Drosophila, that the expression of genes involved in the generation of neurons and muscle contraction decreases with age, that the expression levels of genes involved in reproduction and metabolism increase with age, and that the expression of a number of genes is associated with mating and reproduction.

(1) the transcriptome of ant queens is highly dynamic with age, and (2) this dynamic is characterized by a set of age-related expression changes that is shared with flies, but also by a set of expression changes that is specific to ants.

(i) we compared whole-body transcriptomes from differently aged queens of Cardiocondyla obscuroir, (ii) we identified several developmental processes as common signatures of age, (iii) we show that genes associated with reproduction are upregulated, and genes associated with metabolism and muscle contraction are downregulated in old compared to young queens, and (iv) we identified 21 genes that are consistently more highly expressed and associated with lifespan in short-lived, compared to long-lived mated queens.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fecundity / longevity trade off is not a universal rule, and that it depends on the organism and its life history strategy.
the fecundity and longevity trade-off does not apply to ant queens.

the lack of the trade-off between fertility and longevity is not a result of a specific molecular pathway but is rather due to an alternative regulation of the same pathways that are involved in the regulation of fertility and longevity in other organisms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lack of the trade-off in ant queen life histories is not due to a lack of the trade-offs in their gene expression.
the lack of the fertility/longevity tradeoff in queens of eusocial insects can be attributed to alternative regulation of consensually aging-related processes.
aging is not only a general process that affects all organisms but that aging also has a specific molecular signature in each individual organism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the exceptional relationship between fertility and longevity in ant queens is due to alternative regulation of conservatively expressed genes.

the exceptional longevity of ant queens is not the result of a unique set of genes that is not found in other organisms but is the outcome of a specific regulatory program that leads to the alternative expression of conserved genes.

the lack of a negative correlation between fertility and longevity in ants is not a consequence of the absence of the molecular mechanisms that underlie aging and reproduction in other organisms, but instead results from the alternative regulation of these mechanisms in ants.
